solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Head in old coin (5)

blocks.note: the top of the head, as in a hat fitting at that spot
a pre-decimal British coin worth five shillings

annotation.surface: A monarch's head stamped on an old coin.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a portrait on a coin, and both halves are the answer. A crown was a British coin worth five shillings, a quarter of a pound.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the crown is the top part of the head.

entries.clue: Selfish driver who may sound like a bore? (4,3)

annotation.definition: Selfish driver who may sound like a bore?

blocks.note: a motorist who takes more than a fair share of the lane

blocks.clueFragment: who may sound like a bore?
blocks.note: not a tedious talker: a bore sounds like a boar, the wild pig, which is a kind of swine

annotation.surface: A tedious motorist who drones on behind the wheel.
annotation.walkthrough: A hog is a pig, like a boar, so the selfish motorist is a road hog, and a boar is what 'bore' sounds like; the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a road hog is a motorist who hogs the road, driving selfishly.

entries.clue: Person flogging fish is an impudent type (14)

blocks.note: the snapper is a sea fish

annotation.surface: A cheeky fishmonger shouting his wares at the market.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flogging fish' reads as selling fish at a stall; here flogging means whipping, and the fish is a separate item.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a whippersnapper is a young and presumptuous person.

entries.clue: Precious metal consumed stone (5)

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

annotation.surface: Someone swallowed a valuable piece of metal and a pebble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Precious metal' could be gold (AU) or silver (AG); only silver's symbol fits here.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: agate is a banded semi-precious stone.

entries.clue: Leave wife and split costs (2,5)

blocks.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney for one's wife

annotation.surface: A divorce: walking out on your wife and dividing the bills.
annotation.walkthrough: Dutch for wife comes from Cockney 'my old Dutch' (short for duchess), a London working-class term of affection for a wife.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to go Dutch is to have each person pay their own share.

entries.clue: Fairy tale featuring Jack’s beanstalk, perhaps? (4,5)

annotation.definition: Fairy tale featuring Jack’s beanstalk, perhaps?

blocks.note: read as a children's story, but also any far-fetched, untrue account
the beanstalk grows up to the clouds, so this is a story about something of great height

annotation.surface: Jack and the Beanstalk introduced as a fairy tale.
annotation.walkthrough: Jack and the Beanstalk is literally a story about something tall, and it is also far-fetched, which is what a tall story is.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a tall story is an exaggerated, hard-to-believe account, much like a fairy tale.

entries.clue: Swallow feathers (4)

blocks.note: the verb, as in gulping a pint in one go
the soft fine feathers of a bird, used to fill duvets

annotation.surface: A swallow's plumage.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes Swallow the bird, owning the feathers; it is the verb, as in downing a pint.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are plain senses: to swallow quickly, and a bird's soft under-plumage.

entries.clue: Living ingredients in a pudding? (5-3-6)

blocks.note: the noun, a livelihood: the basic work that pays the bills
a traditional British baked dessert is named after its two main ingredients

annotation.surface: Wondering what live things might be in a pudding.
annotation.walkthrough: Living is the noun, a livelihood, not the adjective. Bread and butter pudding is a British dessert of buttered bread baked in custard.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the work that earns one's basic income is one's bread and butter.

entries.clue: TV show Israel broadcast (6)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: to broadcast is to scatter, so the letters are strewn about

annotation.surface: A television programme aired by Israel.
annotation.walkthrough: Broadcast sits beside TV so naturally it reads as airing; it originally meant sowing seed by scattering.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a programme told in instalments is one kind of TV show.

entries.clue: Many staff and I go out of business (8)

blocks.note: a firm that folds goes out of business

annotation.surface: A worker and many colleagues losing their jobs as the firm closes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Many staff' looks like a single phrase about a big workforce; Many is the definition and staff starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly literary: 'many-fold' means numerous and varied.

entries.clue: Drink spiked by king, more significant (6)

indicatorNotes.spiked by: a drink spiked by something has it slipped inside

annotation.surface: A royal slipping something into a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Spiking a drink means adding something to it, which is exactly what a container does to the outer word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: bigger, in the sense of mattering more.

entries.clue: Maestro, foremost of composers, I’ll give you a lift! (6)

indicatorNotes.foremost of: the foremost letter of a word is its first

blocks.note: 'Hop in!' is what a driver offering a lift says

annotation.surface: A driver cheerfully offering a great composer a ride.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation is a spoken phrase to be replaced by another: someone offering a lift says 'Hop in!'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Polish pianist-composer is one maestro.

entries.clue: Where devil lives, I am Satan transformed (8)

indicatorNotes.transformed: the letters are changed into a new form

annotation.surface: The Devil announcing himself in a new guise, with Hell as his home.
annotation.walkthrough: The devil is not Satan but the Tasmanian devil, a small fierce marsupial found only on that Australian island.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the island is the only wild home of the marsupial called the devil.

entries.clue: Savage sharing decorative food (7)

indicatorNotes.Savage: to savage is to maul, so the letters are torn about

annotation.surface: Fierce squabbling over a plate of decorative nibbles.
annotation.walkthrough: Savage looks like an adjective describing the sharing; it is the instruction to maul the letters of the next word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: food added to a dish for decoration or flavour.

entries.clue: Feeling at home with training (9)

annotation.surface: Feeling comfortable with a home-study course.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Feeling at home' reads as one phrase meaning comfortable; it splits after Feeling.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a hunch, known without reasoning.

entries.clue: How medicine may be given, failing that partner (6)

annotation.surface: A doctor's instructions: take the medicine, or have your partner give it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Failing that' is a whole phrase standing for one tiny word, the conjunction that offers an alternative.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: by mouth, the usual route for tablets and syrups.

entries.clue: Glossy trap – something attractive (6)

blocks.note: a glossy is a magazine, a mag

annotation.surface: A glossy magazine as a lure for something appealing.
annotation.walkthrough: Glossy looks like an adjective but is the noun for a magazine printed on shiny paper.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on attraction: literally it pulls iron, figuratively it draws people.

entries.clue: Old clothes on – yes! (6)

annotation.definitionNote: an exclamation of assent, used in speech as 'Agreed!'

indicatorNotes.clothes: to clothe something is to wrap it round

annotation.surface: Agreeing to put on some old clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: Clothes is a verb here, and 'on' means concerning, as in memo headers.
annotation.definitionFit: An exclamation of assent, said as a hearty yes.

entries.clue: Major English political party is anxious (5,2)

blocks.note: a major is a musical key
the DUP is Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist Party

annotation.surface: A big English party nervous before an election.
annotation.walkthrough: Major looks like 'big', describing the party; it is the musical key. The DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: wound up tight with nerves, like a tuned string.

entries.clue: Ensure relative remains shut up! (4,3)

blocks.note: read literally: make sure your mother stays

annotation.surface: An order to make a relative stay put, and be quiet about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is read literally, retain plus mother. Mum meaning silent is British usage, as in the wartime slogan 'Be like Dad, keep Mum'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: mum means silent, so the phrase orders silence.

entries.clue: Recognise when ready for mining work? (4,3)

blocks.note: to spot someone in a crowd
a miner's tool drawn and in hand

annotation.surface: Spotting when the miners are about to start digging.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is whimsical, flagged by the question mark: with the pick out, the miner is ready to dig.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb: to single out and identify from among others.

entries.clue: Lead in pencil I gather wrong – it’s a form of carbon (8)

indicatorNotes.Lead in: the lead, or leading letter, of a word is its first
indicatorNotes.wrong: the letters are put in the wrong order

annotation.surface: Someone correcting a belief that pencil lead is actually lead.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a true fact: pencil 'lead' is not lead at all but this carbon. Here 'Lead in' just means the first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the soft grey crystalline carbon used in pencils.

entries.clue: Meal right, pack sandwiches (6)

indicatorNotes.sandwiches: to sandwich something is to put it between two layers

blocks.note: a pack is a bunch, a group

annotation.surface: Planning a picnic: pack the sandwiches for the meal.
annotation.walkthrough: Sandwiches reads as food, fitting Meal; it is a verb here.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the late-morning meal blending breakfast and lunch.

entries.clue: Judicial punishment swift, say (4)

blocks.note: British slang for time served in prison
the swift is one example of a feathered flier

annotation.surface: Calling for justice to be swift.
annotation.walkthrough: Swift looks like an adjective about fast justice; it is the creature. Bird for prison time is British slang, from rhyming slang 'birdlime' = time.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: British slang for a prison sentence, as in 'doing bird'.

entries.clue: Currency in which yours truly invested, the first person from Asia (6)

annotation.definitionNote: adjective phrase for the adjective YEMENI

indicatorNotes.in which: together with 'invested', points to the currency as the outer part
indicatorNotes.invested: money invested is put into something

blocks.note: I is the first person pronoun

annotation.surface: A letter-writer describing a currency they put money in, and the first person to do so from Asia.
annotation.walkthrough: Yemen is on the Arabian Peninsula, which is part of Asia.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: from one country in western Asia.

entries.clue: Two-hour race for some, relative jogged round though (8)

indicatorNotes.round: one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: though shortened by dropping its last three letters UGH, the informal spelling tho'

annotation.surface: Elite runners finish a marathon in two hours, though a relative of mine merely jogged it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For some' makes the definition fair: only the elite finish the 26.2-mile race in about two hours.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the elite finishing time identifies the long-distance road race.

entries.clue: Maxim, a little saying, no meaning (5)

indicatorNotes.a little: only a little of the words is used, the part inside them

annotation.surface: Dismissing a proverb as a little saying with no real meaning.
annotation.walkthrough: Saying, right beside Maxim, looks like the definition; the answer sits inside 'saying, no meaning'. The same word is an old term for an aphorism.
annotation.definitionFit: A rare sense: a short pithy saying, from Greek for opinion.

entries.clue: Reportedly big jar (5)

indicatorNotes.Reportedly: as reported, i.e. as heard spoken

annotation.surface: News of a large storage jar.
annotation.walkthrough: Jar looks like a pot; it is the verb, as in sounds that jar on the nerves.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to have an irritating, rasping effect.
